bibl.title: Differential Receptive Field Properties of Parvalbumin and Somatostatin Inhibitory Neurons in Mouse Auditory Cortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how the two main cortical interneuron types differ in what sounds they respond to, once they are identified genetically rather than by spike shape
span.quote: In auditory cortex, however, functional properties of genetically identified inhibitory neurons are poorly characterized. By two-photon imaging-guided recordings, we specifically targeted 2 major types of cortical inhibitory neuron, parvalbumin (PV) and somatostatin (SOM) expressing neurons, in superficial layers of mouse auditory cortex.

span.label: whether parvalbumin and somatostatin neurons in auditory cortex have different frequency tuning, thresholds and timing from each other and from excitatory cells
span.quote: The recent development of inhibitory-cell-type-specific transgenic mouse lines ( Taniguchi et al. 2011 ) opens a new window for in vivo identification of inhibitory neurons.

span.label: shows PV cells are broadly tuned with low thresholds and fast responses while SOM cells are as selective as excitatory neurons and markedly delayed, and traces the difference to input range and input-output efficiency
span.quote: We found that PV cells exhibited broader tonal receptive fields with lower intensity thresholds and stronger tone-evoked spike responses compared with SOM neurons. The latter exhibited similar frequency selectivity as excitatory neurons.

span.label: existence
span.quote: We found that PV cells exhibited broader tonal receptive fields with lower intensity thresholds and stronger tone-evoked spike responses compared with SOM neurons.

span.label: tonal receptive fields of cortical inhibitory interneuron subtypes
span.quote: Here in the mouse primary auditory cortex (A1), we performed in vivo two-photon imaging-guided targeted cell-attached and whole-cell recordings from PV and somatostatin (SOM) expressing neurons, 2 major types of cortical inhibitory neuron, and compared their frequency–intensity tonal receptive fields (TRFs) of spike output and synaptic input.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: By two-photon imaging-guided recordings, we specifically targeted 2 major types of cortical inhibitory neuron, parvalbumin (PV) and somatostatin (SOM) expressing neurons, in superficial layers of mouse auditory cortex.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: PV neurons pool a wider range of excitatory inputs and receive stronger subthreshold drive, so more of that input crosses spike threshold, producing broad, weakly selective spike tuning
span.quote: The broader/weaker frequency tuning of PV neurons was attributed to a broader range of synaptic inputs and stronger subthreshold responses elicited, which resulted in a higher efficiency in the conversion of input to output.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: SOM spiking is late mainly because the excitatory synaptic input itself arrives late, with longer synaptic integration adding to the delay
span.quote: Therefore, the delayed spiking of SOM neurons could be mainly attributed to their delayed synaptic input, while a longer integration time may also contribute to their late spiking.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Non-selective local connectivity from excitatory cells onto inhibitory (especially PV) cells pools inputs with many different preferred frequencies onto one interneuron
span.quote: which would result in a pooling of excitatory inputs with a wide range of preferred frequencies in layer 2/3 inhibitory cells

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: SOM neurons bypass the direct ascending (feedforward) pathway and are instead driven through slower horizontal circuits, which is why their input is delayed
span.quote: On the other hand, SOM neurons receive delayed excitatory input, suggesting that unlike PV and excitatory neurons, SOM neurons do not receive direct ascending inputs.

span.label: PV cells pool excitatory input from neurons with a wide range of preferred frequencies because excitatory-to-PV connectivity is unselective
span.quote: On the other hand, connectivity between excitatory and inhibitory (in particular PV) neurons is much less selective ( Yoshimura and Callaway 2005 ; Hofer et al. 2011 ; Wilson et al. 2012 ), which would result in a pooling of excitatory inputs with a wide range of preferred frequencies in layer 2/3 inhibitory cells.

span.label: PV cells also convert input to output more efficiently, so a broad input becomes an even broader spike tuning
span.quote: The broader/weaker frequency tuning of PV neurons was attributed to a broader range of synaptic inputs and stronger subthreshold responses elicited, which resulted in a higher efficiency in the conversion of input to output.

span.label: PV cells are driven at the same time as excitatory cells, consistent with shared feedforward input from layer 4
span.quote: PV neurons receive their excitatory drive at the same time as excitatory neurons, and their spiking activity occurs before excitatory neurons. These results suggest that PV neurons, similar as excitatory cells, receive feedforward ascending inputs, likely from layer 4

span.label: SOM cells receive delayed input, suggesting horizontal rather than ascending drive
span.quote: On the other hand, SOM neurons receive delayed excitatory input, suggesting that unlike PV and excitatory neurons, SOM neurons do not receive direct ascending inputs. Instead, they are more likely driven by excitation through horizontal circuits

span.label: the two types target different parts of the pyramidal cell - perisomatic for PV, distal dendrite for SOM - which is why they can act on different input streams
span.quote: PV neurons preferentially target perisomatic regions where ascending inputs are most likely located, while SOM neurons preferentially target distal dendritic domains where feedback excitatory inputs are most likely located

span.label: Cells taken as excitatory were unlabelled rather than positively identified, so a minority may be other inhibitory types.
span.quote: The unlabeled neurons were most likely excitatory, although at a low chance (<10%), they could also be one of a variety of unlabeled inhibitory cell types.

span.label: Intensity thresholds are relative, not absolute, because background noise could not be fully removed.
span.quote: It is worth noting that the intensity thresholds being compared are relative rather than absolute thresholds, since, in our current experimental condition, we could not completely eliminate background noise.

span.label: All recordings were made under urethane anaesthesia, and SOM responses in particular may differ in the awake state.
span.quote: Future experiments are required to investigate whether SOM neurons in auditory cortex exhibit higher evoked firing rates in awake states than in anesthesia, and whether the increased firing rates would affect tonal receptive field properties of these cells.

span.label: urethane anaesthesia may suppress SOM cells specifically; in visual cortex their evoked rates fall about tenfold relative to the awake running state while PV rates do not
span.quote: In the visual cortex, it is suggested that SOM neurons are more sensitive to anesthesia than PV and pyramidal neurons: sensory-evoked firing rates of SOM neurons are reduced about 10-fold in urethane anesthesia when compared with the awake running state, while the firing rates of PV neurons are not different between anesthesia and running conditions

span.label: intensity thresholds are relative, not absolute, because background noise could not be fully eliminated
span.quote: It is worth noting that the intensity thresholds being compared are relative rather than absolute thresholds, since, in our current experimental condition, we could not completely eliminate background noise.

span.label: the unlabelled comparison cells are only most likely excitatory, with under a 10% chance of being an unlabelled interneuron type
span.quote: The unlabeled neurons were most likely excitatory, although at a low chance (<10%), they could also be one of a variety of unlabeled inhibitory cell types.

span.label: the Gaussian bandwidth measure fits many PV cells poorly because their tuning is plateau-shaped, and 67% fall below R squared 0.3
span.quote: It should be noted that the plateau shape of frequency tuning of many PV cells makes it fit poorly into a Gaussian curve (67% of PV cells displaying R 2 < 0.3). Following Moore and Wehr (2013) study, we excluded cells with R 2 < 0.2. But including all cells did not affect our conclusion.

span.label: whether SOM receptive fields look different in awake animals is left for future work
span.quote: Future experiments are required to investigate whether SOM neurons in auditory cortex exhibit higher evoked firing rates in awake states than in anesthesia, and whether the increased firing rates would affect tonal receptive field properties of these cells.

span.label: Cre driver lines crossed to a reporter, so that a cell's type is known before it is recorded rather than inferred after
span.quote: The recent development of inhibitory-cell-type-specific transgenic mouse lines ( Taniguchi et al. 2011 ) opens a new window for in vivo identification of inhibitory neurons.

span.label: imaging-guided targeted recording of identified interneuron types, and the expectation that PV cells are less selective
span.quote: In auditory cortex, however, functional properties of genetically identified inhibitory neurons are poorly characterized. By two-photon imaging-guided recordings, we specifically targeted 2 major types of cortical inhibitory neuron, parvalbumin (PV) and somatostatin (SOM) expressing neurons, in superficial layers of mouse auditory cortex.

span.label: SOM
span.quote: In the visual cortex, it is suggested that SOM neurons are more sensitive to anesthesia than PV and pyramidal neurons: sensory-evoked firing rates of SOM neurons are reduced about 10-fold in urethane anesthesia when compared with the awake running state, while the firing rates of PV neurons are not different between anesthesia and running conditions

span.label: urethane
span.quote: In the visual cortex, it is suggested that SOM neurons are more sensitive to anesthesia than PV and pyramidal neurons: sensory-evoked firing rates of SOM neurons are reduced about 10-fold in urethane anesthesia when compared with the awake running state, while the firing rates of PV neurons are not different between anesthesia and running conditions

span.label: PV and SOM here are GENETIC identities - Cre driver lines crossed to a fluorescent reporter and confirmed by dye co-localisation - not waveform classes
span.quote: The co-localization of red and green fluorescence indicated that the desired inhibitory cell was correctly targeted

span.label: fast-spiking is NOT interchangeable with PV: 13% of SOM cells here had trough-to-peak intervals under 0.5 ms, and the cited work reports the PV and pyramidal waveform distributions overlap much more than assumed
span.quote: This issue was further complicated by a recent study ( Moore and Wehr 2013 ) showing that parvalbumin (PV) inhibitory neurons, which are commonly thought to correspond to fast-spiking units, and pyramidal neurons have much larger overlapping distributions of spike-waveform parameters than previously indicated.

span.label: spike-width classification is valid HERE and the paper says for what: 'for cell-attached recording in layer 2/3' - a scope, not a general licence
span.quote: These data indicate that for cell-attached recording in layer 2/3, TPI of spike waveform can be used as a criterion to isolate inhibitory neurons with a reasonable accuracy.

span.label: bandwidth is measured three ways in this paper - BW10, BW50% of an envelope fit, and the sigma of a Gaussian fit - and the third is adopted only to match the study being disputed
span.quote: Following the method used in the Moore and Wehr study, we, however, reached the same conclusion that tuning bandwidth of PV cells was broader than SOM and excitatory cells (PV: 1.17 ± 0.10 octave; SOM: 0.52 ± 0.09 octave; Exc: 0.55 ± 0.09 octave. ANOVA and Tamhane test, P < 0.001 between PV and SOM; P < 0.001 between PV and Exc; P > 0.05 between SOM and Exc).

span.label: intensity threshold here is relative to an unremovable noise floor, so the numbers are comparable within this study and not against absolute-threshold work
span.quote: It is worth noting that the intensity thresholds being compared are relative rather than absolute thresholds, since, in our current experimental condition, we could not completely eliminate background noise.

span.label: contradicts → Moore and Wehr (2013) on PV frequency tuning breadth
span.quote: The discrepancy between Moore and Wehr study and our current result may be due to different targeting methods (optogenetics aided indirect targeting vs. visually guided direct targeting).

span.label: replicates → Moore and Wehr (2013) on PV intensity tuning
span.quote: Nevertheless, PV neurons showed significantly lower ISIs than excitatory cells ( P < 0.01, K–S test), indicating that PV neurons were less intensity-tuned, which is consistent with the observation in a recent study ( Moore and Wehr 2013 ).

span.label: builds-on → Wu et al. (2008) intracellular study of rat auditory cortex layer 4
span.quote: Supporting this notion, our previous intracellular study in layer 4 of the rat auditory cortex indicates that the frequency range of synaptic input is similar between fast-spiking cells and pyramidal neurons, although the spike response range is still broader in the former cells due to a higher efficiency in converting input to spike out ( Wu et al. 2008 ).

span.label: contradicts → Moore and Wehr 2013, which reported PV neurons as sharply tuned as excitatory cells in the same species and area
span.quote: However, a recent study also in mouse auditory cortex reported that PV neurons were as sharply tuned for frequency as excitatory cells ( Moore and Wehr 2013 ). In that study, tuning bandwidth was compared by fitting the frequency-dependent responses with a Gaussian function.

span.label: critiques → spike-waveform identification of inhibitory neurons in extracellular recording
span.quote: Previously, fast-spiking putative inhibitory units have been isolated based on their narrow spike waveforms. These units differ from regular-spiking (putative excitatory) units at some aspects of response and receptive field properties. For example, fast-spiking units have broader spectral tuning and shorter response latencies compared with regular-spiking cells ( Atencio and Schreiner 2008 ; Wu et al. 2008 ). However, the spike-waveform-based identification of putative inhibitory neurons is imperfect ( Andermann et al. 2004 ; Barthó et al. 2004 ). Some pyramidal cells may also have short-duration action potentials that may create classification errors

span.label: confirms → fast-spiking-cell reports of broad frequency tuning, some with morphological confirmation
span.quote: Again, BW50% of PV cells was at least twice as broad as those of SOM and excitatory neurons (Fig. 4 C ). These 2 measures of frequency tuning all indicated that PV neurons were less frequency-selective than SOM and excitatory neurons. Therefore, they could readily provide broadly tuned inhibition to excitatory cells.

span.label: extends → visual cortex findings that PV neurons are less stimulus-selective than excitatory cells
span.quote: We found that PV cells exhibited broader tonal receptive fields with lower intensity thresholds and stronger tone-evoked spike responses compared with SOM neurons. The latter exhibited similar frequency selectivity as excitatory neurons.

span.label: builds-on → their own layer 4 intracellular work, where input range was similar but spike range still broader in fast-spiking cells
span.quote: Supporting this notion, our previous intracellular study in layer 4 of the rat auditory cortex indicates that the frequency range of synaptic input is similar between fast-spiking cells and pyramidal neurons, although the spike response range is still broader in the former cells due to a higher efficiency in converting input to spike out

span.label: fast-spiking —distinct-from→ PV
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — CRITERION: the two are commonly equated, and the cited work shows PV and pyramidal waveform distributions overlap much more than assumed. 13% of SOM cells here also spike narrowly
span.quote: This issue was further complicated by a recent study ( Moore and Wehr 2013 ) showing that parvalbumin (PV) inhibitory neurons, which are commonly thought to correspond to fast-spiking units, and pyramidal neurons have much larger overlapping distributions of spike-waveform parameters than previously indicated.

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · trough-to-peak interval —operationalised-as→ PV
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED. The old span named neither. This clause names both and states the identification criterion - PV cells are recognised BY their trough-to-peak interval. — strength of the relation: 0.8 — SCOPED: valid 'for cell-attached recording in layer 2/3'. The same criterion in extracellular unit recording is what the paper criticises
span.quote: These data indicate that for cell-attached recording in layer 2/3, TPI of spike waveform can be used as a criterion to isolate inhibitory neurons with a reasonable accuracy.

span.label: PV —contrasted-with→ SOM
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — CRITERION: broader tuning, lower threshold, stronger and earlier responses - four separable measures, all differing
span.quote: We found that PV cells exhibited broader tonal receptive fields with lower intensity thresholds and stronger tone-evoked spike responses compared with SOM neurons. The latter exhibited similar frequency selectivity as excitatory neurons.

span.label: RETRACTED (`same-as` ASSERTED FROM EQUALITY ON ONE PROPERTY) · SOM —same-as→ excitatory neurons
span.note: RETRACTED: `same-as` ASSERTED FROM EQUALITY ON ONE PROPERTY. The span: 'PV neurons had TRFs twice as broad as those of SOM and excitatory neurons, while THE LATTER 2 DID NOT DIFFER IN THEIR TRF BANDWIDTHS.' SOM cells and excitatory neurons are not the same thing; they failed to differ on a SINGLE MEASURE, in a sentence whose subject is PV. `same-as` is the strongest claim in the vocabulary and it is here standing on one bandwidth comparison. A category claim is relative to the features tested (Somogyi2005/Raposo2014), and this one names its feature in its own span. — strength of the relation: 0.5 — the record marks this weak — same FREQUENCY SELECTIVITY only; they differ in threshold, timing and jitter. A partial identity, weighted low on purpose
span.quote: On average, PV neurons had TRFs twice as broad as those of SOM and excitatory neurons, while the latter 2 did not differ in their TRF bandwidths

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · PV —operationalised-as→ feedforward inhibition
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED. The old span described the timing of PV excitatory drive without naming feedforward inhibition. This sentence names both and states what PV neurons PROVIDE - 'broadly tuned, feedforward inhibition for a rapid control of ascending inputs'. — strength of the relation: 0.9 — the role is inferred from timing - PV cells are driven with excitatory cells and spike before them
span.quote: PV neurons receive their excitatory drive at the same time as excitatory neurons, and their spiking activity occurs before excitatory neurons. These results suggest that PV neurons, similar as excitatory cells, receive feedforward ascending inputs, likely from layer 4

span.label: SOM —part-of→ distal dendrites
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — subcellular target is what lets the two types act on different input streams
span.quote: PV neurons preferentially target perisomatic regions where ascending inputs are most likely located, while SOM neurons preferentially target distal dendritic domains where feedback excitatory inputs are most likely located

span.label: layer 4 —causes→ PV
span.quote: PV neurons receive their excitatory drive at the same time as excitatory neurons, and their spiking activity occurs before excitatory neurons. These results suggest that PV neurons, similar as excitatory cells, receive feedforward ascending inputs, likely from layer 4

span.label: urethane —causes→ SOM
span.note: status: BORROWED: reported of the VISUAL cortex and cited, not measured in this paper's auditory recordings · direction on the measure: reduces · strength of the relation: 0.8 — SIGN: suppressive, and selectively so - about tenfold in visual cortex while PV rates are unchanged. The main scope limit on this record
span.quote: In the visual cortex, it is suggested that SOM neurons are more sensitive to anesthesia than PV and pyramidal neurons: sensory-evoked firing rates of SOM neurons are reduced about 10-fold in urethane anesthesia when compared with the awake running state, while the firing rates of PV neurons are not different between anesthesia and running conditions

span.label: Gaussian —operationalised-as→ tonal receptive field
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.5 — the record marks this weak — a measure adopted for comparability that fits the object badly - 67% of PV cells below R squared 0.3 because their tuning is plateau-shaped
span.quote: It should be noted that the plateau shape of frequency tuning of many PV cells makes it fit poorly into a Gaussian curve (67% of PV cells displaying R 2 < 0.3). Following Moore and Wehr (2013) study, we excluded cells with R 2 < 0.2. But including all cells did not affect our conclusion.

span.label: cell-attached —part-of→ two-photon
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — imaging guides the pipette; dye co-localisation afterwards is what confirms the right cell was held
span.quote: The co-localization of red and green fluorescence indicated that the desired inhibitory cell was correctly targeted

span.label: intensity threshold —operationalised-as→ SOM
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.7 — SOM thresholds are higher, which is read as an inability to inhibit at low sound levels
span.quote: The intensity threshold of SOM neuron TRFs was significantly higher than PV and excitatory neurons (Fig. 4 D ), suggesting that SOM neurons may not be able to provide inhibition under low-intensity stimuli.

span.label: trough-to-peak interval —operationalised-as→ PV
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — RE-GROUNDS Li2015-differential-receptive-field-properties-of-p[1]: the relation was always stated, the endpoint names were not in the span.
span.quote: we found that spike waveforms of all the recorded PV cells exhibited a trough-to-peak interval (TPI) shorter than

span.label: PV —operationalised-as→ feedforward inhibition
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — RE-GROUNDS Li2015-differential-receptive-field-properties-of-p[4]: the old span named ONE endpoint.
span.quote: PV neurons can provide broadly tuned, feedforward inhibition for a rapid control of ascending inputs to excitatory neurons through somatic integration, possibly resulting in a gain modulation of spike responses of excitatory neurons ( Atallah et al.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and post hoc test was used to compare the means of multiple groups.

span.label: post hoc test
span.quote: In the case of equal variance, post hoc Fisher's least significant difference test was applied; otherwise, Tamhane's T 2 test was applied.

span.label: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
span.quote: Kolmogorov–Smirnov test (K–S test) was applied to test the statistical difference between distributions.

span.label: bootstrap
span.quote: Bootstrap sampling (bootstrap, MATLAB, 1000 times) ( Li et al. 2012 ) was applied to determine the statistics of ratio between spike and excitatory post-synaptic potential (EPSP) frequency range.

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: Data were presented as mean ± SE if not otherwise specified.

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: we calculated jitters of response timing from repetitions of CF-tone-evoked spike responses as the standard deviation of first-spike timing

span.label: curve fitting (Gaussian fit, coefficient of determination)
span.term: curve fitting (Gaussian fit, coefficient of determination)
span.quote: We also quantified the bandwidth of iso-intensity frequency tuning curves using σ of a Gaussian fit to the tuning curve, following Moore and Wehr (2013) study.

span.label: p-value
span.quote: The 3 recorded cell groups did not differ in the distribution of characteristic frequencies (7–21 kHz, P > 0.9, K–S test between each pair of cell groups).

span.label: one-way analysis of variance
span.quote: As for response level, PV neurons displayed much higher tone-evoked firing rates than SOM and excitatory cells (Fig. 2 C ). In addition, the spontaneous firing rate of PV neurons was significantly higher than excitatory cells and tended to be higher than SOM neurons

span.label: K–S test
span.quote: The 3 recorded cell groups did not differ in the distribution of characteristic frequencies (7–21 kHz, P > 0.9, K–S test between each pair of cell groups).

span.label: Tamhane
span.quote: Following the method used in the Moore and Wehr study, we, however, reached the same conclusion that tuning bandwidth of PV cells was broader than SOM and excitatory cells (PV: 1.17 ± 0.10 octave; SOM: 0.52 ± 0.09 octave; Exc: 0.55 ± 0.09 octave. ANOVA and Tamhane test, P < 0.001 between PV and SOM; P < 0.001 between PV and Exc; P > 0.05 between SOM and Exc).

span.label: Bootstrap sampling
span.quote: Intensity selectivity index (ISI) was calculated as 1 minus the ratio between the spike count at 30 dB above the preferred intensity or the highest intensity tested and that at the preferred intensity (i.e., the intensity that produced maximum spike count).

span.label: Parvalbumin (PV) inhibitory neurons in layer 2/3 auditory cortex have broader tonal receptive fields, lower intensity thresholds and stronger tone-evoked spiking than somatostatin (SOM) neurons.
span.quote: We found that PV cells exhibited broader tonal receptive fields with lower intensity thresholds and stronger tone-evoked spike responses compared with SOM neurons.

span.label: SOM neurons are as sharply frequency-tuned as excitatory neurons even though they too receive a broad range of excitatory input.
span.quote: SOM neurons, although also receive a broad range of inputs, display similar frequency selectivity as excitatory neurons.

span.label: Both the synaptic input onset and the spike onset of SOM neurons occur significantly later than those of PV and excitatory neurons.
span.quote: In addition, onsets of both the input and spike responses of SOM neurons were significantly delayed compared with PV and excitatory cells.

span.label: Measured 10 dB above threshold, PV receptive fields were twice as broad as those of SOM and excitatory neurons, which did not differ from each other.
span.quote: On average, PV neurons had TRFs twice as broad as those of SOM and excitatory neurons, while the latter 2 did not differ in their TRF bandwidths

span.label: SOM neurons required significantly louder tones to respond than PV or excitatory neurons, implying they cannot supply inhibition at low sound intensities.
span.quote: The intensity threshold of SOM neuron TRFs was significantly higher than PV and excitatory neurons

span.label: SOM neurons fired with significantly less precise timing, showing larger first-spike jitter than PV and excitatory neurons.
span.quote: SOM neurons had significantly larger jitters of first-spike timing compared with PV and excitatory neurons

span.label: PV neurons converted almost their whole synaptic input range into spike output (highest spike-range/input-range ratio), whereas SOM neurons converted the least.
span.quote: Overall, the ratio of spike tuning range over input range was the highest for PV neurons, and lowest for SOM neurons

span.label: Tone-evoked subthreshold depolarizations (EPSPs) were significantly larger in PV neurons than in SOM or excitatory neurons.
span.quote: Notably, the amplitude of EPSPs was significantly larger in PV than SOM and excitatory neurons, as shown by the rightward shift of the cumulative distribution of EPSP amplitudes

span.label: Every recorded PV cell had a spike trough-to-peak interval below 0.5 ms while every recorded excitatory cell was above 0.5 ms, so waveform width separates the two classes in layer 2/3.
span.quote: Similarly, we found that spike waveforms of all the recorded PV cells exhibited a trough-to-peak interval (TPI) shorter than 0.5 ms, while those of all the recorded excitatory neurons had TPIs longer than 0.5 ms

span.label: PV neurons fired spontaneously at a significantly higher rate than excitatory cells.
span.quote: the spontaneous firing rate of PV neurons was significantly higher than excitatory cells and tended to be higher than SOM neurons

span.label: The three cell groups were recorded at statistically indistinguishable cortical depths, so the broad PV tuning is not a depth-sampling artefact.
span.quote: Finally, the 3 cell groups did not differ significantly in their distributions of cortical depths

span.label: PV receptive fields were about twice as broad as SOM and excitatory ones, which did not differ from each other
span.quote: On average, PV neurons had TRFs twice as broad as those of SOM and excitatory neurons, while the latter 2 did not differ in their TRF bandwidths

span.label: the same result held for a second bandwidth measure taken from an envelope fit
span.quote: Again, BW50% of PV cells was at least twice as broad as those of SOM and excitatory neurons (Fig. 4 C ). These 2 measures of frequency tuning all indicated that PV neurons were less frequency-selective than SOM and excitatory neurons. Therefore, they could readily provide broadly tuned inhibition to excitatory cells.

span.label: PV cells fired much faster to tones than SOM or excitatory cells, and had higher spontaneous rates
span.quote: As for response level, PV neurons displayed much higher tone-evoked firing rates than SOM and excitatory cells (Fig. 2 C ). In addition, the spontaneous firing rate of PV neurons was significantly higher than excitatory cells and tended to be higher than SOM neurons

span.label: SOM cells had higher intensity thresholds, so they may not inhibit at low sound levels
span.quote: The intensity threshold of SOM neuron TRFs was significantly higher than PV and excitatory neurons (Fig. 4 D ), suggesting that SOM neurons may not be able to provide inhibition under low-intensity stimuli.

span.label: SOM cells had larger first-spike jitter than PV or excitatory cells
span.quote: In addition, we calculated jitters of response timing from repetitions of CF-tone-evoked spike responses as the standard deviation of first-spike timing. SOM neurons had significantly larger jitters of first-spike timing compared with PV and excitatory neurons

span.label: spikes occur in the order PV, excitatory, SOM, with SOM markedly delayed
span.quote: Spike responses of these neurons are evoked in a PV-excitatory-SOM neuron sequence, with SOM neuron responses markedly delayed relative to PV and excitatory neurons.

span.label: all PV cells had trough-to-peak intervals under 0.5 ms and all excitatory cells above, but 13% of SOM cells also fell under
span.quote: Similarly, we found that spike waveforms of all the recorded PV cells exhibited a trough-to-peak interval (TPI) shorter than 0.5 ms, while those of all the recorded excitatory neurons had TPIs longer than 0.5 ms (Fig. 2 A , B ). The majority of SOM neurons had TPIs longer than 0.5 ms, while a small percentage (13%) exhibited TPIs shorter than 0.5 ms

span.label: PV cells were less intensity-tuned than excitatory cells
span.quote: Nevertheless, PV neurons showed significantly lower ISIs than excitatory cells ( P < 0.01, K–S test), indicating that PV neurons were less intensity-tuned, which is consistent with the observation in a recent study

span.label: ADOPTED THE RIVAL'S METHOD: fitting bandwidth by Gaussian as the disputing study did, the disagreement survived - PV tuning was still broader
span.quote: Following the method used in the Moore and Wehr study, we, however, reached the same conclusion that tuning bandwidth of PV cells was broader than SOM and excitatory cells (PV: 1.17 ± 0.10 octave; SOM: 0.52 ± 0.09 octave; Exc: 0.55 ± 0.09 octave. ANOVA and Tamhane test, P < 0.001 between PV and SOM; P < 0.001 between PV and Exc; P > 0.05 between SOM and Exc).

span.label: three candidate causes remain for the disagreement: indirect optogenetic versus direct visual targeting, contamination in tungsten electrode recording, and general versus premapped A1
span.quote: The discrepancy between Moore and Wehr study and our current result may be due to different targeting methods (optogenetics aided indirect targeting vs. visually guided direct targeting). One concern about the tungsten electrode recording approach as in Moore and Wehr study is the potential contaminations from other types of units of nearby neurons. This potential problem perhaps can be prevented by coupling cell-attached loose-patch recordings with optogenetic identification, as cell-attached recording is more reliable than single-unit recording in faithfully picking up spike signals only from the patched individual neuron ( Wu et al. 2008 , 2011 ; Zhou et al. 2012 ). Additionally, in the Moore and Wehr study, the auditory cortex was generally recorded, while, in this study, we specifically targeted certain areas of premapped A1.

span.label: CONTROL NULL: the three cell groups did not differ in characteristic frequency distribution
span.quote: The 3 recorded cell groups did not differ in the distribution of characteristic frequencies (7–21 kHz, P > 0.9, K–S test between each pair of cell groups).

span.label: CONTROL NULL: the three groups did not differ in cortical depth, so the tuning difference is not a sampling bias
span.quote: Finally, the 3 cell groups did not differ significantly in their distributions of cortical depths (Fig. 4 H ), indicating that the difference in frequency tuning between PV and other cell types cannot be attributed to a sampling bias of PV cells at a particular cortical depth.

span.label: CONTROL: the imaging laser and chiller were isolated and no scanning occurred during recording, so scanner noise could not contaminate auditory responses
span.quote: To circumvent any impacts of background noise on auditory responses, our imaging and recording system was custom-built in a sound-attenuation room, with the pumping laser and chiller isolated from the room (Fig. 1 A ). In addition, laser scanning and imaging was performed only for guiding the electrode to patch onto a cell before any auditory responses were recorded. This avoided the relatively high-level noise emitted from the scanning mirrors.

span.label: characteristic frequency (CF)
span.quote: Characteristic frequency (CF) was defined as the frequency (Hz) at which the lowest sound pressure level was necessary to evoke a significant excitatory response.

span.label: intensity threshold
span.quote: Intensity threshold was defined as the minimum intensity to evoke a significant excitatory response.

span.label: bandwidth of the tonal receptive field (BW10)
span.term: bandwidth of the tonal receptive field (BW10)
span.quote: Bandwidth of TRF was determined as the total frequency range for effective tones, at the intensity level of 10 dB above the threshold (i.e., BW10), or at 60-dB SPL.

span.label: intensity selectivity index (ISI)
span.quote: Intensity selectivity index (ISI) was calculated as 1 minus the ratio between the spike count at 30 dB above the preferred intensity or the highest intensity tested and that at the preferred intensity

span.label: onset latency of spike response
span.quote: Onset latency of spike response was determined from the generated peristimulus spike time histogram (PSTH) as the lag between the stimulus onset and the time point where spike rate exceeded the average baseline by 2 standard deviations of baseline fluctuations.

span.label: characteristic frequency
span.quote: Characteristic frequency (CF) was defined as the frequency (Hz) at which the lowest sound pressure level was necessary to evoke a significant excitatory response. Intensity threshold was defined as the minimum intensity to evoke a significant excitatory response.

span.label: tonal receptive field
span.quote: A threshold at the value equal to the spontaneous spike rate plus 20% of the peak-evoked rate was then used to define significant evoked responses. Responses to frequency–intensity combinations that met this criterion were considered to fall within the TRF of the neuron, which generated the contour of the TRF

span.label: intensity selectivity index
span.quote: Intensity selectivity index (ISI) was calculated as 1 minus the ratio between the spike count at 30 dB above the preferred intensity or the highest intensity tested and that at the preferred intensity (i.e., the intensity that produced maximum spike count).
